overview:
Most visitors to Merzouga see only the dunes of the Erg Chebbi. This private day trip goes the other way, across the black stone plain of the hamada to Safsaf, a small "wild" oasis hidden in a narrow rocky gorge about 45 km from Merzouga, near the Algerian border. A stream runs between the walls of the gorge, lined with date palms and small gardens, and after rain it spills over little waterfalls into clear pools. Few tours come here, so you usually share it only with the families who farm it and their goats.

The day is as much about the journey as the oasis. Your 4x4 follows desert tracks past nomad tents, acacia trees and dry riverbeds, with stops to look for fossils in the stone and to hear how people live in this part of the Tafilalet. At Safsaf your local guide walks with you through the palm gardens, explains how water from the stream is shared between families by a traditional rota, and how the gardens are planted in three layers – palms on top, fruit trees below, vegetables and barley on the ground. Lunch is a simple home-cooked meal with a local family, and on the way back you stop in an earthen ksar village before returning to Merzouga in the afternoon.

AT A GLANCE
• Duration: about 6 hours (morning start, back by mid-afternoon)
• Start and finish: your hotel or camp in Merzouga or Hassi Labied
• Distance: about 45 km each way, mostly on desert tracks
• Type: private 4x4 trip with driver and local guide
• Walking: about 2–3 km on flat but narrow garden paths and the stream bed
• Activity level: easy; the tracks are bumpy
• Languages: English, French or Spanish; Arabic and Berber locally

WHAT YOU SEE
• The hamada: the vast black-stone desert that surrounds the dunes, with nomad camps and acacias.
• Fossil beds in the limestone, where shells and orthoceras show the area was once a sea.
• Safsaf gorge: palms, gardens, a stream and, in wetter months, small waterfalls and pools.
• Traditional irrigation: open channels and the shared water rota that keeps the oasis alive.
• An earthen ksar village and its narrow covered lanes.

WHY THIS TRIP WORKS
It shows the side of the desert most travellers miss: not sand, but stone, water and the oasis farming that has supported people here for centuries. It fits well on a free morning between a camel trek and your onward journey, and the shaded gardens are a welcome change after a day in the dunes.

WHO WILL ENJOY IT
Travellers spending two nights or more in Merzouga, photographers, families, walkers, and anyone curious about how people actually live in the Sahara.

WHO MIGHT PREFER ANOTHER TOUR
For the dunes, Khamlia's Gnawa music and the fossil workshops in one day, take the [4x4 desert tour around the Erg Chebbi](/en-US/morocco/merzouga/tours/merzouga-4x4-desert-tour-around-erg-chebbi-khamlia-gnawa-music-fossils/40c42a5360a6b1d9b6cbceb4). For a night in the dunes, see the [overnight camel trek with sunset and sunrise](/en-US/morocco/merzouga/tours/overnight-camel-trekking-in-merzouga-sunset-ride-desert-camp-and-sunrise/cdba9d9aa746e1f5add261ba).

PRACTICAL INFORMATION
Wear closed shoes or sandals that can get wet, a hat and sunscreen, and bring water and a light layer (mornings are cold in winter). Bring cash for lunch with the family and tips. The flow of the stream depends on the season: the waterfalls are best after the autumn and winter rains and may be only a trickle in late summer, but the gardens are green all year.
descriptions:
What to expect: a private 4x4 day across the stony desert to a hidden palm oasis in a gorge, with a local guide, a family lunch and a ksar village on the way back.

Your driver and local guide pick you up at your hotel or camp in the morning. Leaving the dunes behind, the 4x4 heads out onto the hamada, a plain of dark stones that stretches to the horizon. The tracks cross dry riverbeds, pass groups of acacia trees and the brown tents of nomad families who move with their goats and camels, and climb onto low rocky ridges. Along the way you stop where the limestone is full of fossils – spiral ammonites and long orthoceras from a sea that covered this land hundreds of millions of years ago – and your guide explains how the local fossil trade works.

After about an hour and a half you reach Safsaf. The oasis sits in a narrow gorge where a stream comes out of the rock, and suddenly the desert gives way to palms, reeds and green garden plots. You walk along the stream with your guide, crossing the water on stones, past small pools and, when there has been rain, little waterfalls. The gardens are farmed by a handful of families: dates on top, pomegranate, fig and olive trees in the middle, and vegetables, barley and alfalfa on the ground. Water is led through earth channels and each family's turn is measured by time; your guide shows you the gates and explains how disputes are settled.

Around midday you sit down with a local family for a simple home-cooked lunch – usually a vegetable tagine or madfouna, the stuffed bread of the Tafilalet, with dates and mint tea. On the return you stop at an earthen ksar, a fortified village of mud-brick houses with covered lanes and a shared granary, before arriving back in Merzouga in the mid-afternoon, in time to rest before a sunset camel ride.

SCHEDULE (times are estimates; in summer we start earlier)
09:00 – Pick-up at your hotel or camp in Merzouga or Hassi Labied.
09:30 – 4x4 across the hamada, nomad camps and a fossil stop (about 1.5 hours with stops).
11:00 – Walk through the Safsaf gorge, gardens and stream with your guide (about 1.5 hours).
12:30 – Lunch with a local family (about 1 hour, not included).
13:30 – Drive back with a stop in an earthen ksar village (about 1 hour).
15:00 – Drop-off at your hotel or camp.

GOOD TO KNOW
• The oasis is a working farm and a home: stay on the paths, ask before picking fruit and before photographing people.
• The tracks are rough; tell us if anyone suffers from back problems or motion sickness.
• The stream can be crossed on stones but feet may get wet; bring shoes you don't mind getting muddy.
• After heavy rain some tracks can be closed; your driver chooses another route or we move the trip to another day.

INCLUDED: private 4x4 vehicle and driver, local guide, bottled water, pick-up and drop-off in Merzouga.
NOT INCLUDED: lunch with the family (paid locally), tips.

IF THE WEATHER TURNS: in summer heat we leave at 08:00 and spend more time in the shade of the gorge; on windy days with blowing sand the fossil stop is shortened. Strong rain can close the tracks, in which case we offer another date.

WHAT YOU'LL TASTE
Dates from the oasis (the Tafilalet grows Medjool and Boufeggous), a vegetable tagine or madfouna with the family, fresh bread and mint tea.

PHOTO SPOTS
• The black hamada with the dunes on the horizon.
• Light filtering through the palms over the stream.
• Reflections in the pools and the waterfalls after rain.
• Earthen walls of the ksar against the green gardens.

ACCESSIBILITY
The garden paths are flat but narrow and sometimes muddy near the channels; reaching the falls means stepping over stones. The 4x4 ride is bumpy. Tell us about mobility needs and we can keep the walk short.

WHAT YOU TAKE AWAY: the other face of the Sahara – stone, water and the patient oasis farming that makes life possible here.

faq.question: Where is the Safsaf oasis?
faq.answer: About 45 km from Merzouga, reached by 4x4 tracks across the hamada towards the Algerian border. It lies in a narrow rocky gorge where a stream feeds palm gardens. The drive takes about an hour and a half with stops.

faq.question: How long is the trip?
faq.answer: About 6 hours: a morning start around 09:00 and back in Merzouga around 15:00. In summer we start earlier to avoid the heat.

faq.question: Are there really waterfalls?
faq.answer: Yes, small ones, but they depend on the season. After the autumn and winter rains the stream flows strongly over the rocks; in late summer it can be just a trickle. The palm gardens are green all year.

faq.question: Can we swim?
faq.answer: In wetter months there are small pools where you can paddle or cool off. The water is not deep, and please respect the families' gardens and water channels.

faq.question: Is lunch included?
faq.answer: No. A simple home-cooked lunch with a local family is arranged and paid locally; it is a modest amount and goes directly to the family. Vegetarian food is easy.

faq.question: Is the trip private?
faq.answer: Yes. The 4x4, driver and guide are only for your group, so you can stay longer at the oasis or skip a stop.

faq.question: Is it suitable for children?
faq.answer: Yes. Children enjoy looking for fossils, crossing the stream and seeing the animals. The tracks are bumpy, so very young children should be comfortable in the car.

faq.question: Is it hot?
faq.answer: From May to September the desert is very hot by midday, so we leave early. The gorge and palm gardens are shaded and cooler. In winter mornings are cold; bring a warm layer.

faq.question: What is a ksar?
faq.answer: A fortified village of mud-brick houses built close together behind a wall, with covered lanes, a mosque and a shared granary. Ksour were built for protection and to keep the oasis harvest safe.

faq.question: How is the water shared?
faq.answer: By a traditional rota: each family has the right to the water for a set time, opening small earth gates to flood their plots. Your guide explains how the turns are measured and how the system is managed.

faq.question: What should I wear?
faq.answer: Light, covering clothes, a hat and sunscreen, and closed shoes or sandals that can get wet. A scarf helps if the wind blows sand.

faq.question: Can I do it on the same day as a camel trek?
faq.answer: Yes. The trip ends around 15:00, in time to rest before a sunset camel ride to a desert camp.

faq.question: What happens if it rains?
faq.answer: Heavy rain is rare but can make some desert tracks impassable. Your driver will take another route if possible; otherwise we move the trip to another day.
